stem: A defining strength of a prospective cohort design, relative to a case-control design, is that it:
options: is well suited to studying a rare disease efficiently
selects participants purely on the basis of their current outcome status
establishes that exposure preceded outcome, supporting temporality
measures past exposure by asking participants to recall it
rationale: A cohort follows exposed and unexposed groups forward, so exposure is recorded before the outcome occurs and temporality is secured. Selecting on outcome status describes a case-control design. Efficiency for rare diseases is a case-control strength, since a cohort would need to be very large. Relying on recalled past exposure is also a case-control feature and a source of recall bias.

stem: The case-control design is generally the most efficient choice when the outcome under study is:
options: rare, because cases can be assembled directly rather than waited for
best measured by randomly allocating the exposure
expected to change exposure status repeatedly over time
common, so that many cases accrue quickly in a followed cohort
rationale: Sampling on the outcome lets a case-control study gather enough cases of a rare condition without following a huge population. A common outcome is handled well by a cohort, which would accrue cases quickly. Repeatedly changing exposure suits a design that tracks people over time, not outcome-based sampling. Randomly allocating exposure describes a trial, not an observational case-control study.

stem: Temporality, as a consideration in causal inference, refers to whether:
options: the association holds consistently across different populations
a dose-response gradient is present across exposure levels
the putative cause can be shown to precede the effect in time
the exposure and outcome are measured on the same individuals
rationale: Temporality is the requirement that the cause come before the effect; without it a causal claim cannot stand. Measuring both on the same individuals is just a feature of many designs, not temporality. A dose-response gradient is a separate consideration in causal reasoning. Consistency across populations speaks to external validity rather than to time order.

stem: An ecological study differs from a cohort or case-control study principally because its unit of analysis is:
options: the time interval, with the same group compared against itself
the individual, with each single person's exposure and outcome paired
the group or population, with exposure and outcome measured as aggregates
the matched pair, with one exposed and one unexposed member
rationale: An ecological study relates group-level exposure rates to group-level outcome rates, so the unit is the population rather than the person. Pairing each individual's own exposure and outcome describes individual-level designs. A matched pair is a feature of matched case-control studies. Comparing a group against itself over intervals describes a time-based design, not the ecological unit.

stem: An analyst notes that regions with higher average salt intake also have higher average stroke rates, and wants to claim that individuals with high salt intake are at higher stroke risk. The main limitation of drawing that individual-level conclusion from this design is:
options: proportional hazards being violated in the survival model used
the ecological fallacy, since a group-level association need not hold for individuals
recall bias, since each person reported their own salt intake from memory alone
loss to follow-up, since some whole regions were not tracked to the study's end
rationale: Moving from a group-level association to a claim about individuals is the ecological fallacy: the relationship between averages need not describe any person. Recall bias would require individual self-report, which an aggregate design does not use. Loss to follow-up is a cohort problem and does not apply to aggregate regional data. A proportional-hazards concern belongs to survival modelling, not to this comparison of regional averages.

stem: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is most useful in study design because it helps the analyst to:
options: test whether the residuals from a fitted regression are normally distributed
allocate participants randomly between exposure groups
decide which variables to adjust for and which to leave alone
estimate the magnitude of an effect once all the data have been collected and cleaned
rationale: A DAG encodes assumed causal relationships, which guides which variables are confounders to adjust for and which are colliders or mediators best left alone. It does not itself estimate effect sizes; that comes from the analysis. Checking residual normality is a model diagnostic unrelated to the graph. Random allocation is a feature of trial design, not of causal diagrams.

stem: Investigating whether a workplace exposure causes a slowly developing cancer with a long latency, a team wants exposure recorded before disease onset but cannot wait decades. The design that best balances temporality with feasibility here is:
options: a case series describing the features of patients who already have the cancer
an ecological comparison of cancer rates across differently exposed regions
a retrospective cohort, using past exposure records to follow people to outcome
a cross-sectional survey measuring exposure and disease at a single time point
rationale: A retrospective cohort uses historical exposure records as the starting point and follows people to the outcome, preserving exposure-before-outcome order without waiting in real time. A cross-sectional survey measures both at once and cannot establish which came first. An ecological comparison works on group rates and risks the ecological fallacy. A case series has no comparison group and cannot support a causal claim.

stem: A weakness shared by cross-sectional designs when used for causal questions is that they:
options: can only be conducted once a rare outcome has been assembled as cases
require very long follow-up before any outcome can be observed
depend on randomly allocating the exposure to participants
measure exposure and outcome simultaneously, leaving time order ambiguous
rationale: Because a cross-sectional study captures exposure and outcome at the same moment, it usually cannot say which preceded the other, undermining temporality. Long follow-up is a cohort burden, not a cross-sectional one. Assembling cases first describes case-control sampling. Random allocation belongs to experimental designs, not cross-sectional surveys.

stem: Confounding is best described as a distortion of an exposure-outcome association that arises when a third factor is:
options: sitting on the causal pathway between the exposure and the outcome
associated with the exposure and an independent cause of the outcome
measured with error in a way unrelated to either variable
a consequence of both the exposure and the outcome jointly
rationale: A confounder is linked to the exposure and is itself a cause of the outcome by a route other than the exposure, which biases the observed association. A factor on the causal pathway is a mediator, which should usually not be adjusted away. A common consequence of both is a collider, adjustment for which can introduce bias. Error unrelated to either variable describes non-differential measurement error, a separate issue.

stem: A study finds coffee drinkers have more lung cancer. Coffee drinkers are also more likely to smoke, and smoking causes lung cancer. Smoking here is best described as:
options: an effect modifier that changes the coffee effect across strata
a mediator on the causal pathway from coffee to lung cancer
a collider influenced by both coffee and lung cancer
a confounder of the coffee and lung cancer association
rationale: Smoking is associated with coffee drinking and independently causes lung cancer, so it confounds the crude association. It is not a mediator, since coffee does not cause lung cancer through making people smoke. It is not a collider, as it is not a shared consequence of coffee and cancer. Effect modification would mean the coffee effect itself differs across smoking strata, which is a different claim from confounding.

stem: Compared with observational designs, the distinctive causal strength of randomisation is that it:
options: balances only those confounders the analyst has chosen to measure
removes the need to consider temporality in the analysis
tends to balance both measured and unmeasured confounders across groups
guarantees that the two groups have identical outcomes at baseline
rationale: Random allocation distributes confounders, including ones the analyst never measured, evenly across groups on average, which observational adjustment cannot do. It does not make outcomes identical at baseline; outcomes are what the study measures. It does not remove temporality, which randomised designs still respect. Balancing only measured confounders describes regression or matching, not randomisation.

stem: A case-control study is particularly vulnerable to one threat that a prospective cohort largely avoids, namely:
options: the need for an extremely large sample to capture a rare outcome
ambiguous time order because exposure and outcome are measured at once
recall bias, because exposure is ascertained after the outcome is known
loss to follow-up over a long observation period
rationale: Because cases already have the outcome when their past exposure is collected, their recall may differ systematically from controls, producing recall bias. Loss to follow-up is a cohort problem, since case-control studies do not follow people forward. Needing a huge sample for a rare outcome is a cohort limitation that case-control sampling specifically avoids. Ambiguous time order is a cross-sectional weakness, not a defining case-control one.

stem: Recall bias is best described as a systematic error that arises when:
options: the accuracy of remembered exposure differs between those with and without the outcome
an association seen at group level is wrongly applied to individuals
participants are selected into the study in a way related to both exposure and outcome
a measuring instrument consistently reads higher or lower than the true value
rationale: Recall bias occurs when people with the outcome remember past exposures differently from those without it, distorting the comparison. Selection into the study related to exposure and outcome is selection bias. A measuring instrument that reads consistently off describes measurement or instrument bias. Misapplying a group-level association to individuals is the ecological fallacy.

stem: Measurement bias differs from random measurement error principally because measurement bias:
options: arises only when the sample size is too small to be representative
pushes values systematically in one direction rather than scattering them
always makes the confidence intervals far narrower than they really should be
describes applying a population-level finding to an individual
rationale: Measurement bias is systematic: the error tends in a consistent direction and shifts estimates away from the truth, whereas random error scatters values around it. It does not reliably narrow confidence intervals; random error tends to widen them. Small sample size relates to random sampling error, not to directional measurement bias. Applying a population finding to an individual is the ecological fallacy.

stem: Sampling error, as distinct from bias, refers to the variation in an estimate that arises because:
options: the analysis was applied to the wrong unit of observation
the measuring procedure systematically favours higher readings
participants who remained in the study differ from those who left
a sample, rather than the whole population, has been observed
rationale: Sampling error is the random difference between a sample estimate and the true population value that comes simply from observing a subset; larger samples reduce it. A procedure that systematically favours higher readings is measurement bias, which is directional rather than random. Differences between stayers and leavers describe attrition, a form of selection bias. Using the wrong unit of observation is an ecological issue, not sampling error.

stem: In a survey of past diet, women who have had a child with a birth defect describe their pregnancy diets in far more detail than mothers of healthy children. The most relevant threat to validity is:
options: overdispersion, since the count data vary more than the model expects
confounding, since a third factor causes both diet and the defect
ecological fallacy, since a group rate is being read onto individuals
recall bias, since outcome status has shaped how exposure is remembered
rationale: Mothers of affected children recalling their diet differently from other mothers is recall bias, driven by knowledge of the outcome. The ecological fallacy concerns group-to-individual inference, which is not what is happening here. Overdispersion is a property of count-data models, not a recall problem. Confounding would involve a third causal factor, but the issue described is differential memory, not a common cause.

stem: A false positive in a statistical test corresponds to:
options: an estimate that is precise but centred away from the true value
failing to detect an effect that is genuinely present
an interval that is too wide to be informative
concluding an effect is present when in truth there is none
rationale: A false positive, or type I error, is declaring an effect that does not really exist. Failing to detect a real effect is a false negative, or type II error. An estimate that is precise but off-centre describes bias, not a test error. An over-wide interval reflects imprecision, which is a separate matter from a false positive.

stem: Increasing a study's sample size, all else equal, chiefly reduces:
options: random error, narrowing confidence intervals around the estimate
systematic measurement bias built into the instrument
confounding by factors associated with both exposure and outcome
selection bias introduced by how participants were recruited
rationale: A larger sample reduces random error, so estimates become more precise and intervals narrower. It does not fix a biased instrument, which mismeasures every observation in the same direction however many there are. It does not remove selection bias, which is baked in by recruitment. It does not address confounding, which persists regardless of sample size and needs design or analysis to control.

stem: External validity refers to the extent to which a study's findings:
options: generalise to populations or settings beyond the one studied
rest on a correctly specified statistical model
are free of systematic error within the study sample itself
reach conventional levels of statistical significance
rationale: External validity is about generalisability: whether results transfer to other people, places or conditions. Freedom from systematic error within the sample is internal validity, a different property. Correct model specification is an analytical concern, not generalisability. Reaching significance speaks to the strength of evidence within the study, not to whether it applies elsewhere.

stem: A trial of a treatment is run entirely in fit volunteers aged 20 to 40, then its results are promoted for use in frail patients over 80. The most direct concern is:
options: recall bias, since participants reported their own symptoms
a false negative, since the trial may well have missed a genuine real effect
overdispersion in the outcome counts collected during the trial
limited external validity, as the studied group differs from the target
rationale: Applying results from young, fit volunteers to frail elderly patients stretches the findings beyond the studied population, which is an external validity problem. A false negative concerns missing a real effect within the study, not transfer to a new group. Recall bias would need differential memory of past exposure, which is not the issue here. Overdispersion is a modelling property of counts, unrelated to generalising across age groups.

stem: A false negative, in contrast to a false positive, occurs when an analysis:
options: yields a confidence interval that excludes the null
declares an effect that does not in fact exist
produces an estimate biased away from the true value
fails to detect an effect that genuinely exists
rationale: A false negative, or type II error, is missing a true effect, often because power is too low. Declaring an effect that is not there is a false positive. An estimate biased away from the truth is a question of accuracy, not of a missed detection. An interval excluding the null indicates a detected effect, the opposite of a false negative.

stem: Selection bias is best understood as a distortion that arises when:
options: an estimate varies from the truth purely because a sample was taken
a gauge consistently records values above the true reading
entry into or retention in a study relates to both exposure and outcome
respondents with the outcome recall their exposures more completely
rationale: Selection bias arises when entry into or retention in the study depends on a mix of exposure and outcome, so the studied group is unrepresentative in a way that distorts the association. Differential recall of exposure by outcome status is recall bias. A gauge reading consistently high is measurement bias. Variation from the truth due simply to sampling is random sampling error, not selection bias.

stem: An online health survey is shared mainly through fitness forums, and the analyst then reports the national prevalence of regular exercise as very high. The most relevant problem is:
options: a false positive, since the test wrongly found an effect
selection bias, since recruitment favoured people likely to exercise
measurement bias, since the instrument read systematically high
violation of proportional hazards in the survival analysis
rationale: Recruiting through fitness forums brings in people more likely to exercise, so the sample is unrepresentative and prevalence is overstated: this is selection bias. A false positive concerns a hypothesis test wrongly finding an effect, not a skewed sample. Measurement bias would mean the instrument itself mis-records, which is not what recruitment did. Proportional hazards is a survival-model assumption with no bearing on a prevalence survey.

stem: The ecological fallacy is the error of:
options: remembering past exposures differently according to outcome status
concluding an effect exists when in reality it does not
selecting participants in a manner linked to exposure and outcome
drawing conclusions about individuals from group-level associations
rationale: The ecological fallacy is drawing individual-level conclusions from group-level data, where the relationship between aggregates need not hold for any person. Selecting participants in a way tied to exposure and outcome is selection bias. Concluding an effect exists when it does not is a false positive. Differential recall of exposure by outcome is recall bias.

stem: The linearity assumption in an ordinary linear regression states that:
options: the outcome values are drawn from a normal distribution at every predictor level
the mean of the outcome changes by a constant amount per unit of the predictor
the variance of the errors is the same across all predictor values
the observations are independent of one another
rationale: Linearity means a one-unit change in the predictor is associated with the same change in the expected outcome throughout its range. Normality of the outcome at each predictor level is a separate, distributional assumption. Independence of observations is its own requirement. Equal error variance across predictor values is homoscedasticity, again distinct from linearity.

stem: The proportional hazards assumption, central to certain survival analyses, requires that:
options: the ratio of hazards between groups stays constant over follow-up time
censoring occurs at exactly the same rate in each group
the hazard in every group falls steadily as time passes
the survival times themselves follow a normal distribution across groups
rationale: Proportional hazards means the hazard ratio comparing groups does not change as time goes on, even though the underlying hazards may rise or fall. It does not require survival times to be normal; survival data are typically skewed and censored. It does not require hazards to fall over time, only that their ratio be stable. Equal censoring rates are not what the assumption states.

stem: In a survival analysis comparing two treatments, the hazard ratio is clearly larger early in follow-up and much smaller later on. This pattern most directly signals a problem with:
options: the proportional hazards assumption, as the hazard ratio shifts over time
the linearity assumption, since the predictor effect is not a straight line
the independence assumption, since observations appear correlated
the normality assumption, since residuals depart from a bell shape
rationale: A hazard ratio that drifts with time violates proportional hazards, which assumes the ratio holds steady across follow-up. Linearity concerns how a continuous predictor maps to the outcome, not how a ratio behaves over time. Independence concerns correlation between observations, which is not what changing hazards shows. Normality of residuals is a regression diagnostic, not the issue with a time-varying hazard ratio.

stem: The independence assumption is most clearly threatened when data are:
options: measured on a predictor that relates non-linearly to the outcome
drawn from a distribution that is skewed rather than symmetric
clustered, such as repeated measurements taken on the same patients
counts whose variance exceeds the mean assumed by the model
rationale: Repeated measures on the same individuals are correlated, so observations are not independent and standard errors computed under independence are wrong. A non-linear predictor relationship is a linearity problem, not an independence one. Counts with variance above the mean indicate overdispersion. A skewed distribution concerns the shape of the data, separate from whether observations are independent.

stem: Overdispersion, in the context of count-data models, describes the situation where:
options: the hazard ratio between groups shifts across the follow-up period
the observed variance is greater than the model assumes for the mean
the predictor and outcome are related by a curved rather than straight line
successive observations on a unit are correlated over time
rationale: Overdispersion means the data vary more than a model such as Poisson expects given the mean, so uncertainty is understated unless it is accommodated. A curved predictor-outcome relationship is a linearity issue. A shifting hazard ratio is a proportional-hazards problem. Correlation between successive observations is a breach of independence, which can coexist with but is not the same as overdispersion.

stem: The normality assumption in standard linear regression most precisely concerns:
options: the constancy of a hazard ratio across follow-up time
the equality of error variance across the range of fitted values
the absence of correlation between successive observations
the distribution of the residuals, rather than the raw predictors
rationale: In ordinary linear regression it is the residuals that are assumed to be approximately normal, not the predictors themselves. Equality of error variance across fitted values is homoscedasticity, a distinct assumption. Absence of correlation between observations is independence. A constant hazard ratio over time is the proportional-hazards assumption from survival analysis.

stem: An analyst models the number of falls per ward per month with a Poisson model, but finds the data vary far more widely than the model's mean-equals-variance expectation. The most accurate description of this problem is:
options: non-normal residuals in an underlying linear model
non-linearity between the chosen predictors and the modelled outcome variable
overdispersion, with variance exceeding what the count model assumes
violation of proportional hazards across the months observed
rationale: Count data varying more than a Poisson model expects is overdispersion, and ignoring it understates uncertainty. Non-linearity is about the functional form linking predictors to outcome, not about excess variance. Proportional hazards belongs to survival analysis, not to monthly count modelling. Non-normal residuals are a linear-regression concern and do not capture the mean-variance mismatch in counts.

stem: Why does violating a method's assumptions matter when interpreting its output? Because violations:
options: convert a cohort design into a case-control design
can bias estimates or distort uncertainty, so conclusions may be misleading
make randomisation unnecessary for controlling measured confounders
always increase the sample size needed to reach statistical significance
rationale: When assumptions fail, point estimates can be biased or standard errors and intervals miscalculated, so the reported conclusion may not be trustworthy. Assumption violations do not simply scale the required sample size in a fixed way. They have nothing to do with making randomisation unnecessary. They certainly do not change one study design into another; design is fixed by how the study was conducted.

stem: Homoscedasticity, an assumption of ordinary linear regression, is best described as:
options: approximate normality of the residual distribution
mutual independence of the individual observations
a constant change in the outcome value per single unit of the predictor
constant variance of the errors across the range of fitted values
rationale: Homoscedasticity means the spread of the errors stays the same across fitted values; when it fails, standard errors can be wrong. A constant change in outcome per unit predictor is linearity. Approximate normality of residuals is the normality assumption. Mutual independence of observations is the independence assumption, each distinct from equal error variance.

stem: A linear regression of cost on age shows residuals that fan out widely at older ages but cluster tightly at younger ages. This pattern most directly indicates a breach of:
options: independence, since observations appear correlated with one another
homoscedasticity, since the error variance is not constant across the range
proportional hazards, since a hazard ratio changes over time
linearity, since the mean relationship clearly is not a straight line at all
rationale: Residuals spreading out at one end and tightening at the other show non-constant error variance, a breach of homoscedasticity. Linearity concerns whether the mean relationship is straight, which the fanning pattern does not by itself establish. Independence concerns correlation between observations, not changing spread. Proportional hazards is a survival-analysis assumption and does not apply to this regression.

stem: Stratification controls confounding by:
options: modelling the outcome on the exposure and confounders together in one equation
summarising each person's confounders into a single probability of exposure
randomly allocating the exposure so that confounders balance out on average
examining the exposure-outcome association separately within levels of the confounder
rationale: Stratification splits the data by confounder level and looks at the association within each stratum, where the confounder is held roughly fixed. Random allocation describes randomisation, a design-stage control. Putting exposure and confounders into one equation is regression adjustment. Collapsing confounders into a single probability of exposure describes a propensity score.

stem: A propensity score summarises, for each individual, the:
options: probability of developing the outcome given the particular exposure received
stratum of the confounder into which the individual falls
probability of receiving the exposure given their measured characteristics
size of the exposure effect estimated within their subgroup
rationale: A propensity score is the modelled probability that a person is exposed given their measured covariates, used to balance groups on those covariates. The probability of the outcome given exposure is a different quantity, closer to a risk. A confounder stratum is what stratification uses, not what a propensity score is. The size of an exposure effect is an output of analysis, not the score itself.

stem: A defining limitation shared by regression adjustment, stratification, matching and propensity scores, but not by randomisation, is that they:
options: make the independence assumption unnecessary in the analysis
require the outcome to be reasonably rare in the wider source population
control just those confounders that have been measured and included
remove the need to consider the temporality of exposure
rationale: All of these analytic methods can only adjust for confounders the analyst measured and entered; unmeasured confounders remain, which is exactly what randomisation handles on average. None of them requires a rare outcome; that is a case-control sampling matter. They do not waive the independence assumption. They do not remove the need to think about temporality, which still matters for causal claims.

stem: Comparing a new surgical technique against an old one using observational records, an analyst pairs each new-technique patient with an old-technique patient of similar age, sex and comorbidity. This approach to controlling confounding is:
options: randomisation, since allocation to technique was left to chance
stratification, since the association was read within confounder bands
matching, since participants are paired on confounder values
regression adjustment, since confounders entered a single model
rationale: Pairing patients with similar confounder profiles across the two groups is matching, which balances those confounders by construction. Randomisation would require chance allocation to technique, which did not happen in these records. Regression adjustment would put the confounders into a model rather than pairing people. Stratification would compute the association within confounder bands rather than forming matched pairs.

stem: Regression adjustment differs from stratification chiefly in that regression:
options: models exposure and confounders jointly, allowing for several at once
balances unmeasured as well as measured confounders by design
discards every participant who cannot be paired with another
examines the association only within a single confounder level at a time
rationale: Regression adjustment puts exposure and confounders into one model, which handles several confounders together and is efficient when stratification would create too many thin strata. Balancing unmeasured confounders is a property of randomisation, not regression. Looking within a single confounder level at a time is stratification. Discarding the unpaired describes a limitation of matching, not regression.

stem: A practical drawback of controlling several confounders by stratification alone is that:
options: it can only ever adjust for a single binary confounder
it requires the proportional hazards assumption to hold
it balances confounders that were never measured by the analyst
strata can become so thin that estimates within them are unstable
rationale: As more confounders are stratified on, the data split into many small strata, and estimates within sparse strata become unstable, which is why regression is often preferred. Stratification cannot balance unmeasured confounders; only randomisation does that on average. It does not depend on proportional hazards, a survival-analysis assumption. It is not limited to one binary confounder, though many confounders strain it.

stem: An analyst wants to adjust for a dozen measured confounders at once in an observational study, but stratifying on all of them would leave almost empty cells. A more workable confounding-control strategy here is:
options: randomisation of the exposure after the data have been collected
restricting analysis to a single stratum of one confounder
a propensity score condensing the measured confounders into one summary
ignoring temporality so that the exposure can be modelled directly
rationale: A propensity score collapses many measured confounders into a single probability of exposure, sidestepping the empty-cell problem of stratifying on all of them. Randomisation cannot be applied after the fact to existing observational data. Ignoring temporality would undermine any causal reading and does not address confounding. Restricting to one stratum of one confounder leaves the other confounders uncontrolled.

stem: Restriction controls confounding by:
options: limiting eligibility to a single level of the confounder so it cannot vary
entering the confounder as a covariate alongside the exposure
allocating the exposure to participants at random
pairing each exposed participant with an unexposed one on the confounder
rationale: Restriction admits only participants at one level of the confounder, so it is constant and cannot distort the association, at the cost of generalisability. Pairing on the confounder is matching. Entering the confounder as a covariate is regression adjustment. Allocating exposure at random is randomisation. Each controls confounding by a different mechanism.

stem: A residual weakness even of a well-fitted propensity-score analysis is that it:
options: requires the outcome to follow a normal distribution
cannot balance confounders that were not measured and entered into the score
removes any need to assess the temporality of the exposure
controls even those confounders the analyst never thought to record or measure
rationale: A propensity score balances only the covariates fed into it, so unmeasured confounders still bias the result, unlike randomisation. It does not control unmeasured confounders; that is the very gap. It does not require a normal outcome. It does not waive temporality, which remains essential to a causal interpretation.

stem: Reviewers note that an observational study adjusted thoroughly for every confounder the team measured, yet they remain uneasy about a confounder no one recorded. The honest analytic response is that:
options: the ecological fallacy explains why the adjustment was unnecessary
regression adjustment will have balanced the unmeasured confounder anyway
a larger sample would have eliminated the unmeasured confounding
measured-confounder methods cannot remove bias from an unmeasured confounder
rationale: Methods that adjust for measured confounders leave unmeasured confounding untouched, so the reviewers' concern is well founded. Regression cannot balance a confounder it never saw. Increasing the sample reduces random error but does nothing to unmeasured confounding. The ecological fallacy is about group-to-individual inference and has no bearing on this adjustment question.

stem: Time-series methods are particularly suited to data that are:
options: aggregate exposure and outcome rates compared across regions
ordered observations of the same measure taken sequentially over time
matched pairs of exposed and unexposed individuals
independent observations from a single cross-sectional snapshot
rationale: Time-series analysis is built for sequential observations of a quantity over time, where order and dependence between successive points matter. A single cross-sectional snapshot has no time ordering. Matched pairs belong to study-design control, not time-series. Comparing aggregate rates across regions is an ecological comparison, not a temporal sequence.

stem: Discrete-event simulation is most appropriate for modelling a system in terms of:
options: transitions of a cohort between a fixed set of health states over cycles
individual entities flowing through queues as distinct events occur
stocks and flows linked by feedback loops at an aggregate level
a single sequence of one measure recorded at regular time intervals
rationale: Discrete-event simulation represents entities, such as patients, moving through a system one event at a time, which suits queueing and resource-use problems. Stocks and flows with feedback loops describe system dynamics. Movement of a cohort between defined health states over cycles describes a Markov model. A single measure recorded at intervals is a time series, not an event-based simulation.

stem: A Markov model represents a process as:
options: transitions between defined states, the next depending on the current
interacting stocks and flows governed by feedback loops
entities queuing for shared resources as individual events unfold over time
a single variable observed in sequence at fixed time points
rationale: A Markov model moves a population between defined states across cycles, with transition probabilities that depend on the present state rather than the full history. Entities queuing for resources as events occur is discrete-event simulation. Interacting stocks and flows with feedback is system dynamics. A single variable observed in sequence is a time series.

stem: System dynamics is distinguished from the other simulation approaches by its focus on:
options: the strengths and limits of odds ratios and confidence intervals
aggregate stocks and flows connected by feedback loops over time
individual entities experiencing discrete events in a queue
a cohort cycling through mutually exclusive health states
rationale: System dynamics models a system at an aggregate level as stocks, flows and feedback loops, capturing how the whole behaves over time. Individual entities and discrete events describe discrete-event simulation. A cohort cycling through health states is a Markov model. Odds ratios and confidence intervals are statistical measures, not a simulation approach.

stem: An analyst wants to model patient waiting times and resource use in an emergency department, tracking individual patients as they arrive, queue, are treated and leave. The most fitting tool is:
options: system dynamics, which models aggregate stocks and feedback loops
discrete-event simulation, tracking individual entities through a queue
a Markov model, which simply moves a cohort between fixed health states
a time-series model of a single measure recorded over time
rationale: Following individual patients through arrival, queueing, treatment and departure is exactly what discrete-event simulation does. A Markov model handles cohort movement between states, not individual queueing dynamics. System dynamics works at an aggregate stock-and-flow level and would not track individual patients. A time series models one measure over time and cannot represent the queueing process.

stem: To estimate long-term costs and outcomes of a chronic disease by moving a cohort between health states such as well, ill and dead over yearly cycles, the natural choice is:
options: a Markov model, which cycles a cohort through defined health states
system dynamics, which models aggregate stocks and feedback loops
a time-series model of a single sequential measure
discrete-event simulation, which follows individual entities through queues
rationale: Cycling a cohort through defined health states over regular periods is the standard use of a Markov model. Discrete-event simulation tracks individuals through events and queues, which is more detail than this cohort-state question needs. System dynamics works with aggregate stocks and feedback rather than discrete health states. A time series models one measure over time and cannot represent state transitions.

stem: A general limitation common to simulation approaches such as discrete-event, system dynamics and Markov models is that their outputs:
options: depend on the structure and parameter assumptions built into the model
remove confounding from the underlying observational data
establish causal effects without needing a comparison group
are entirely free of assumptions once the model has been fully coded
rationale: Every simulation rests on the structural choices and input parameters the modeller specifies, so its outputs are only as sound as those assumptions. They are not assumption-free once coded; the assumptions are embedded. They do not by themselves establish causation. They do not remove confounding from observational inputs; poor inputs propagate into the results.

stem: Choosing a time-series approach over a simple comparison of independent groups is motivated chiefly by the need to:
options: model individual entities moving through a queueing process
summarise measured confounders into a single propensity score
pair each exposed participant with a closely matched unexposed control one
account for dependence and trend between observations ordered in time
rationale: Time-series methods exist because observations taken in sequence are correlated and may trend or cycle, which ordinary group comparisons ignore. Pairing exposed and unexposed participants is matching, a confounding-control method. Modelling entities through a queue is discrete-event simulation. Condensing confounders into a propensity score is an adjustment technique, unrelated to temporal dependence.

stem: A reason the odds ratio is sometimes preferred over the risk ratio is that the odds ratio:
options: is easier for non-technical audiences to interpret intuitively
removes confounding without any need for adjustment
is always numerically equal to the risk ratio regardless of outcome frequency
can be estimated from case-control data, where risks cannot be computed directly
rationale: Because case-control studies sample on outcome, absolute risks are not available, but odds ratios can still be estimated, which is a key strength. The odds ratio is not always equal to the risk ratio; they diverge as the outcome becomes common. It is generally harder, not easier, for lay audiences to interpret than a risk. It does not remove confounding, which still needs design or analytic control.

stem: A recognised limitation of the odds ratio is that it:
options: overstates the risk ratio when the outcome is common
is undefined whenever any exposure group is large
cannot be estimated from case-control study data
is identical to the absolute risk difference
rationale: When the outcome is common, the odds ratio moves further from 1 than the risk ratio, so it can exaggerate the apparent effect if read as a risk ratio. It can in fact be estimated from case-control data, which is one of its strengths. It is not undefined for large groups. It is not the same as the absolute risk difference, which is a different measure on a different scale.

stem: A study of a common outcome reports an odds ratio of 3.0, and a journalist restates this as patients being three times as likely to have the outcome. The most accurate caution is that:
options: the odds ratio and risk ratio always coincide, so the restatement is exact
with a common outcome the odds ratio overstates the risk ratio, exaggerating the effect
the odds ratio measures absolute rather than relative effect, so likelihood language is wrong
the odds ratio cannot be calculated when the outcome is common, so the figure is invalid
rationale: For a common outcome the odds ratio sits further from 1 than the risk ratio, so reading it as a likelihood ratio overstates the effect. The odds ratio can be calculated for common outcomes; the issue is interpretation, not validity. The two ratios do not always coincide; they diverge as the outcome becomes frequent. The odds ratio is a relative, not absolute, measure, so the problem is the magnitude, not the use of relative language.

stem: A 95 per cent confidence interval that excludes the null value indicates that, in conventional terms, the result is:
options: statistically significant, though not necessarily important
a result whose true value is certain to lie inside the interval
free of any systematic bias in how it was estimated
practically important, because the interval is necessarily wide
rationale: An interval excluding the null corresponds to statistical significance at that level, but significance says nothing about whether the effect is large enough to matter. Width relates to precision, not to practical importance, and excluding the null does not make an interval wide. A confidence interval does not certify the absence of bias. It does not place the true value inside with certainty; the confidence level refers to the procedure's long-run coverage.

stem: A wide confidence interval around an estimate primarily signals that the estimate is:
options: imprecise, reflecting substantial random error
biased, reflecting a systematic error in measurement
significant, reflecting a clear departure from the null
confounded, reflecting an uncontrolled third variable
rationale: A wide interval reflects low precision, driven by random error, often from a small sample. Bias is a directional, systematic error and is not what interval width measures. Confounding is a distortion from a third variable, separate from precision. A wide interval that spans the null indicates a lack of significance, not its presence.

stem: Standardised rates are preferred over crude rates when the aim is to:
options: compare populations fairly despite differences in their age structures
remove confounding from an individual-level regression model
avoid any need to choose a reference or standard population
describe the actual overall burden experienced in each population
rationale: Standardisation adjusts for differing age structures so that population comparisons are not driven by age alone, which crude rates cannot do. The crude rate, by contrast, describes the actual overall burden in a population. Standardisation requires choosing a standard population, so it does not avoid that step. It operates on rates, not on individual-level regression adjustment.

stem: Two regions report similar crude mortality rates, but one has a much older population than the other. To compare their mortality fairly, the appropriate step is to:
options: widen the confidence intervals to absorb the age difference
use age-standardised rates to remove the effect of the differing age structures
report odds ratios instead, since they are immune to population structure
compare the crude rates directly, since they already reflect the true burden
rationale: Age-standardised rates adjust both regions to a common age structure, so the comparison is not driven by the older population's age profile. Comparing crude rates directly leaves the age difference in, which is the problem. Odds ratios are not immune to population structure and do not solve the age-mix issue here. Widening intervals changes precision, not the systematic distortion from differing age structures.

stem: A general strength of regression as an analytical method, relative to a simple two-group comparison, is that it:
options: establishes causation directly from observational data
balances confounders that were never measured or recorded by the analyst
can adjust for several variables at once while estimating the exposure effect
is free of any assumptions about the form of the relationship
rationale: Regression can include several covariates together, estimating the exposure effect while adjusting for measured confounders, which a bare two-group comparison cannot. It cannot balance unmeasured confounders; only randomisation does that on average. It does not establish causation by itself from observational data. It is not assumption-free; it relies on assumptions such as the correct functional form.

stem: In K4's terms, a data-driven model is built primarily to:
options: establish the underlying cause of an outcome beyond any reasonable doubt at all
reproduce the source data exactly, leaving no error behind in the fitted model
remove the need for any expert judgement once the model has been built and run
represent activity, financial impact or outcomes to inform a decision
rationale: A model is a deliberate simplification built to support a decision about activity, cost or outcomes; being useful for that decision matters more than being complete. Reproducing the data exactly describes overfitting, not a goal. Models inform judgement rather than replace it, and a data-driven model shows association and supports inference rather than settling causation outright.

stem: A regression model is the natural choice when the task is to:
options: represent a whole system as stocks and flows that feed back on each other
estimate how an outcome relates to one or more predictors
follow a single quantity through time where the order of points matters
build a mechanism from assumed rules and run it forward to see what emerges
rationale: Regression estimates the relationship between an outcome and its predictors. Following an ordered quantity through time is the province of time-series work, building and running a mechanism is simulation, and representing a system as interacting stocks and flows is a simulation approach rather than regression.

stem: Time-series methods are distinguished from ordinary regression chiefly because:
options: they describe association rather than producing any forecast
they assume the relationship between variables is always linear
the data is ordered and that order itself carries information
they need no predictors, working from the outcome alone in every case
rationale: Time-series work adds the complication that points are ordered and each leans on the ones before, so the order carries information. The other options misstate it: time-series methods can use predictors, do not require linearity, and are routinely used to forecast forward.

stem: A simulation differs from a regression or forecasting model because it:
options: builds a mechanism from assumed structure and runs it forward to see what emerges
requires no assumptions, since the behaviour is generated rather than estimated
fits a curve to historical points and reads the trend off that fit
always produces a narrower uncertainty range than a fitted model
rationale: A simulation specifies a mechanism and runs it forward, so results emerge from the assumed structure rather than from a fit to history. Fitting a curve to past points describes forecasting, simulations do not inherently give narrower uncertainty, and they rest heavily on structural assumptions rather than avoiding them.

stem: A team wants to know how a new walk-in clinic would change waiting times before it is built, including queueing for a limited number of staff. There is no historical data for this clinic. The most suitable approach is:
options: a time-series forecast extrapolating the existing site's waiting times
a financial cost-allocation model splitting overheads across clinics
a regression of past waiting times on clinic features at other sites
a simulation that represents the clinic's process and runs it forward
rationale: With no history for the clinic and an interest in how a process with limited resources would behave, building and running a mechanism is the fit. Regression on other sites and a time-series extrapolation both lean on data this clinic does not have, and a cost-allocation model answers a financial question, not a waiting-time one.

stem: An analyst has five years of monthly emergency attendances and is asked to project the next twelve months. The order of the months clearly matters. The most natural approach is:
options: a unit-cost model converting attendances into a budget line
a time-series forecast that uses the ordered history
a cross-sectional regression ignoring the month each value falls in
a simulation of individual patients arriving and being treated
rationale: Ordered monthly history projected forward is the textbook case for a time-series forecast. A simulation would be over-engineering when usable history exists, a regression that ignores the time order discards the very structure that matters, and a unit-cost model answers a budgeting question rather than a projection one.

stem: Saying that forecasting is modelling with time added is meant to convey that:
options: a forecast is inherently more trustworthy than a model because it accounts for time
forecasting takes away the need to think about predictors or modelling assumptions
working with time-ordered data removes the risk of overfitting from the analysis
the usual modelling concerns still hold, with data ordering as an extra complication
rationale: Forecasting keeps every ordinary modelling concern (purpose, predictors, the ways a model can fail) and adds the complication that the data is ordered. It does not remove the need to think about predictors or assumptions, does not make a forecast inherently more trustworthy, and does not protect against overfitting.

stem: An empirical model and a mechanistic model differ mainly in that an empirical model:
options: learns its relationship from data, where a mechanistic model has it specified up front
is reliably more accurate than a mechanistic model when set the very same problem
needs no data of any kind, deriving its entire structure purely from first principles
is restricted to predicting categories and can never return a continuous number
rationale: The defining contrast is where the relationship comes from: an empirical model learns it from data, a mechanistic one has it specified up front. Neither is automatically more accurate, an empirical model does need data, and empirical models predict numbers as well as categories.

stem: A commissioner asks for a model whose internal workings can be inspected and defended in a public decision, even at some cost to raw accuracy. This points towards:
options: the most flexible model on offer, on the view that raw accuracy should always win out
any model at all, on the basis that interpretability and accuracy amount to the same
a simpler, interpretable model, since the decision has to be defensible in public
a model carrying as many predictors as the available data will physically support
rationale: When a decision must be inspected and defended, a simpler interpretable model is the sensible trade, even at some accuracy cost. Always maximising flexibility ignores the defensibility requirement, piling in predictors works against interpretability, and treating interpretability and accuracy as identical misreads the trade-off being made.

stem: The most accurate model is not automatically the most useful because:
options: usefulness rests on fit to the decision and defensibility, not on accuracy alone
usefulness is settled by the size of the dataset rather than by the model itself
accuracy and usefulness are wholly unrelated, so a model's accuracy can be ignored
a more accurate model is reliably too expensive to be worth the effort of building
rationale: Usefulness turns on fit to the decision and defensibility, of which accuracy is only one part. Accuracy is not irrelevant, more accurate models are not always too costly, and usefulness is not simply a function of dataset size.

stem: The linearity assumption in a linear model is the assumption that:
options: the predictors do not carry overlapping information about the outcome
the count outcome's variance does not exceed what the model expects
the relationship between predictor and outcome follows a straight-line form
the spread of the errors stays constant across the range of the predictor
rationale: Linearity is the assumption of a straight-line relationship between predictor and outcome. Constant error spread is homoscedasticity, predictors not overlapping is the absence of multicollinearity, and variance exceeding expectation is overdispersion.

stem: Homoscedasticity refers to the assumption that:
options: no single predictor can be largely predicted from the other predictors in the model
the hazard ratio between the groups being compared stays constant as time passes
the spread of the residuals stays roughly constant across the fitted values
the relationship between predictor and outcome takes a straight-line form throughout
rationale: Homoscedasticity is constant residual spread across the fitted range. A straight-line relationship is linearity, predictors not standing in for each other is the absence of multicollinearity, and a constant hazard ratio over time is the proportional-hazards assumption.

stem: Multicollinearity is present when:
options: the spread of the residuals widens steadily as the fitted value of the outcome increases
two or more predictors carry much the same information, blurring their separate effects
the variance of a count outcome turns out larger than the fitted model actually assumes
the model ends up following the noise in its training data rather than the real signal
rationale: Multicollinearity is predictors carrying overlapping information so their separate effects cannot be separated. Widening residual spread is heteroscedasticity, following the noise is overfitting, and excess count variance is overdispersion.

stem: The proportional-hazards assumption, used in survival models, is that:
options: the outcome variance matches the mean, as a count model expects
the residuals have constant spread across the range of fitted values
each predictor contributes information the others do not
the ratio of the hazard between groups stays constant over time
rationale: Proportional hazards assumes the between-group hazard ratio holds constant over time. Variance matching the mean concerns count models and overdispersion, constant residual spread is homoscedasticity, and predictors contributing distinct information is the absence of multicollinearity.

stem: Overdispersion in a count model means that:
options: the hazard ratio between groups changes as time passes
the observed variance of the counts is greater than the model assumes
the relationship between predictor and outcome curves rather than runs straight
two predictors are so correlated their effects cannot be separated
rationale: Overdispersion is variance in the counts exceeding what the model assumes. A curved relationship is a linearity problem, a changing hazard ratio breaks proportional hazards, and inseparable correlated predictors is multicollinearity.

stem: An overfitted model is one that:
options: carries predictors whose information overlaps too heavily to be told apart cleanly
follows the noise in its training data, so it generalises poorly to new data
is too simple to capture the real pattern that is present in the underlying data
assumes a straight-line relationship where the true relationship is in fact curved
rationale: Overfitting is chasing the noise in the training data so the model travels poorly to new data. Being too simple to catch the pattern is underfitting, assuming a straight line for a curve is a linearity failure, and overlapping predictor information is multicollinearity.

stem: An underfitted model is best described as one that:
options: is too simple to capture the real structure, so it misses the pattern
chases every point in its training data, the random noise very much included
breaks the constant-variance assumption that should hold across the residuals
carries two or more predictors that stand in for one another within the model
rationale: Underfitting is a model too simple to catch the real structure. Chasing every point including noise is overfitting, breaking constant residual variance is heteroscedasticity, and predictors standing in for each other is multicollinearity.

stem: A residual plot shows the scatter of errors fanning out wider and wider as the fitted values increase. The diagnostic concern this points to is:
options: heteroscedasticity, a breach of the constant-variance assumption
multicollinearity, an overlap of information between two predictors
overdispersion, excess variance in a count outcome beyond the model
a failure of the proportional-hazards assumption in a survival model
rationale: Errors fanning out as fitted values grow is the signature of heteroscedasticity, non-constant residual spread. Multicollinearity concerns overlapping predictors, proportional hazards concerns survival models over time, and overdispersion concerns count variance, none of which a fanning residual plot indicates.

stem: A model fits its training data almost perfectly but predicts poorly on data it has not seen. The most likely problem is:
options: a non-linear relationship that has been forced through a straight-line fit
multicollinearity, an information overlap among two or more of the predictors
underfitting, where the model is too simple to capture the real pattern
overfitting, where the model has learned the noise rather than the signal
rationale: Near-perfect training fit with poor performance on new data is the classic mark of overfitting. Underfitting would fit the training data poorly too, multicollinearity affects how effects are attributed rather than producing this split, and forcing a line through a curve is a linearity issue.

stem: Two predictors in a model, household income and area deprivation score, are very strongly related to each other, and the model now gives unstable, hard-to-interpret coefficients for both. The diagnostic at work is:
options: heteroscedasticity, a widening of the residual spread across the fitted values
multicollinearity, since the two predictors carry strongly overlapping information
overfitting, the model having chased the noise present in the training sample
a violation of proportional hazards in the way the groups behave over time
rationale: Two strongly related predictors yielding unstable coefficients is multicollinearity, the overlap making their separate effects hard to pin down. Heteroscedasticity concerns residual spread, overfitting concerns generalisation to new data, and proportional hazards concerns survival models.

stem: When a linear model's assumption is broken, the practical consequence is that:
options: the model becomes more accurate on data it has not seen
the model automatically corrects itself during fitting
the output cannot be taken at face value and may mislead if used unchecked
the breach affects the appearance of the plot but never the conclusions
rationale: A broken assumption means the output cannot be trusted at face value and needs care before use. The model does not self-correct, the breach can change conclusions and not just appearance, and a violated assumption does not improve performance on new data.

stem: An analyst fits a straight line through a relationship that visibly bends, and the residuals show a clear curved pattern rather than scattering randomly. The assumption most directly in question is:
options: homoscedasticity, since the spread of the residuals is visibly changing with x
linearity, since a straight line is being forced through a curved relationship
the absence of multicollinearity between two of the predictors in the model
proportional hazards across the follow-up period of a survival-type analysis
rationale: A curved residual pattern from a straight-line fit signals a linearity failure. Homoscedasticity is about changing spread rather than a curved shape, multicollinearity concerns predictor overlap, and proportional hazards concerns survival timing, none of which a curved residual indicates.

stem: Predictor selection is the task of deciding:
options: which variables go into the model, and on what grounds they earn a place
which states a population is permitted to move between as time passes in a model
how many times a simulation should be re-run before its average can be trusted
how shared overhead costs ought to be split across the services that draw on them
rationale: Predictor selection is choosing which variables enter the model and why. Re-running for a stable average is a simulation concern, splitting overheads is cost allocation, and moving between states is a simulation structure, not predictor choice.

stem: Judging a candidate predictor on plausibility means asking whether:
options: the predictor can be computed quickly when the model runs
the variable has any missing or mismeasured values at all
the variable correlates with at least one other predictor
the relationship makes sense in direction and rough size
rationale: Plausibility asks whether a predictor's relationship to the outcome makes sense in direction and rough magnitude. Missing or mismeasured values is a data-quality concern, computation speed is not a selection criterion here, and correlation with another predictor speaks to multicollinearity rather than plausibility.

stem: Why does the data quality of a predictor matter for selection?
options: a low-quality predictor strengthens the case for adding more predictors
missing or mismeasured values corrupt what the model draws from it
poor data quality makes the model fit its own training set more tightly
data quality bears on the outcome variable but never on the predictors
rationale: Data quality matters because missing or mismeasured values feed corruption downstream into anything the model learns from that predictor. Poor quality does not helpfully tighten the fit, it does not argue for adding more predictors, and it matters for predictors as much as for the outcome.

stem: An interaction between two predictors means that:
options: one predictor has many missing values across the sample
the effect of one predictor depends on the value of another
the two predictors carry the same information as each other
the two predictors must always be entered as a single combined variable
rationale: An interaction is when one predictor's effect depends on the level of another. Carrying the same information is multicollinearity, missing values is a data-quality issue, and an interaction does not require collapsing the two into one variable.

stem: The relevance of a candidate predictor concerns whether:
options: it shares its information with a second predictor
it can be measured without any error in the dataset
its effect depends on the level of another predictor
it has a defensible bearing on the outcome being modelled
rationale: Relevance is whether a predictor has a defensible bearing on the outcome. Error-free measurement is a data-quality matter, an effect depending on another predictor is interaction, and sharing information with a second predictor is multicollinearity.

stem: The claim that more predictors is not necessarily better rests on the fact that:
options: a model can only really be considered valid with a single predictor in it
adding predictors reliably reduces a model's accuracy on its training data
added predictors bring overlap, interaction and a stronger pull to overfit
extra predictors tend to make the underlying data easier to collect cleanly
rationale: Adding predictors brings three new ways to go wrong: overlap, interaction and a stronger pull to overfit, so more is not automatically better. Extra predictors do not always reduce training accuracy, models are routinely valid with several predictors, and adding predictors does not ease data collection.

stem: An analyst proposes adding a predictor that is recorded for only a third of patients and is known to be entered inconsistently where it is recorded. The strongest objection on selection grounds is:
options: relevance, since a variable of this kind cannot bear on the outcome being modelled
data quality, since the sparse, inconsistent values would corrupt what the model draws
implausibility, since no variable recorded in this way could relate to the outcome
interaction, since the effect of this predictor would have to depend on another one
rationale: Sparse and inconsistently entered values is a data-quality objection: the corruption flows downstream. Nothing here shows an interaction, the variable is not shown to be implausible, and no case has been made that it is irrelevant; the stated problem is the quality of its values.

stem: A model of treatment response includes both a drug-dose predictor and an age predictor, and the analyst suspects the dose effect is larger in older patients than younger ones. This suspicion is specifically about:
options: multicollinearity, since dose and age would be carrying the same information
the data quality of the age variable as it has been recorded in the dataset
an interaction, since the effect of dose appears to depend on patient age
the plausibility of including the dose predictor in this model in the first place
rationale: A dose effect that changes with age is an interaction, one predictor's effect depending on another's value. Multicollinearity would mean dose and age overlap in information, data quality concerns measurement of age, and plausibility concerns whether dose belongs at all, none of which is the point here.

stem: In financial modelling of a service, a fixed cost is one that:
options: is shared out across services according to an allocation rule
does not change with the volume of activity over the relevant range
is the cost of treating one more patient beyond the current level
rises in direct proportion to each additional unit of activity
rationale: A fixed cost holds steady as activity varies over the relevant range. Costs that rise with each unit are variable, the cost of one more patient is marginal, and costs shared by a rule are allocated overheads.

stem: When modelling the cost of a service, a variable cost is one that:
options: is split across departments using an agreed allocation basis
stays the same regardless of how much activity takes place
is fixed per unit by national tariff and cannot move
rises and falls with the volume of activity
rationale: A variable cost moves with activity volume. A cost that stays the same regardless of activity is fixed, a cost split across departments is allocated, and a nationally fixed tariff is a unit price set externally rather than the definition of a variable cost.

stem: In financial modelling, the marginal cost of an activity is:
options: the cost of producing one more unit of that activity
the total cost divided by the number of units produced
the portion of shared overhead assigned to that activity
the cost that stays constant as activity changes
rationale: Marginal cost is the cost of one additional unit. Total cost divided by units is the unit or average cost, the share of overhead assigned is cost allocation, and the cost that stays constant is a fixed cost.

stem: In a costing model, the unit cost of a service is best described as:
options: the rule by which overheads are divided between services
the average cost attributed to one unit of activity
the cost that does not vary as activity rises or falls
the cost of the very next unit beyond current activity
rationale: Unit cost is the average cost carried by one unit of activity. The cost of the next unit is marginal, the cost that does not vary is fixed, and the rule for dividing overheads is cost allocation.

stem: In financial modelling, cost allocation refers to:
options: dividing shared or overhead costs across the services that draw on them
the rise in cost that comes from serving one additional patient beyond now
the part of a cost that stays constant regardless of the volume of activity
the total cost of a service expressed per unit of the activity it delivers
rationale: Cost allocation is dividing shared overheads across the services using them. The increase from one more patient is marginal cost, the cost constant with volume is fixed cost, and total cost per unit is unit cost.

stem: In a service costing model, an activity-shift impact is the financial effect of:
options: a change in the national unit price of a procedure
the residual error left after the model is fitted
moving activity from one setting or service to another
a predictor and an outcome moving together over time
rationale: An activity-shift impact is the financial consequence of moving activity between settings or services. A change in national price is a tariff change, predictor and outcome moving together is statistical association, and residual error is a modelling diagnostic, not a financial concept.

stem: A finance analyst is modelling a hospital ward. The building's heating and the salaried core staff stay the same whether the ward runs at 70 percent or 95 percent occupancy. In the cost model, these are:
options: allocated costs, since they are shared out across several wards
fixed costs, since they do not change with the level of activity
variable costs, given that the ward's occupancy level is changing
marginal costs, since they reflect the cost of each extra patient
rationale: Costs that hold steady as occupancy varies are fixed costs. They are not variable, since they do not move with activity, not marginal, since they are not the cost of an extra patient, and the scenario does not describe them being shared out across wards.

stem: In a costing model, an analyst wants the cost of admitting just one more patient to a ward that already has space, heating and staff in place. The concept being asked for is:
options: the unit cost taken as an average across all admissions
the allocated overhead share carried by the ward itself
the fixed cost of keeping the ward open and running
the marginal cost, the cost of that one further admission
rationale: The cost of one more admission, given capacity already in place, is the marginal cost. The fixed cost is what runs regardless of that patient, the unit cost is the average across all admissions rather than the next one, and allocated overhead is the ward's share of shared costs.

stem: A financial model proposes moving a clinic's follow-up appointments out of hospital and into community settings, and estimates the resulting change in cost across both settings. This estimate is an example of:
options: running a sensitivity analysis
calculating a fixed cost
setting a national unit cost
modelling an activity-shift impact
rationale: Estimating the cost effect of moving appointments between settings is modelling an activity-shift impact. It is not a fixed-cost calculation, it is not setting a national unit price, and it is not a sensitivity analysis, which would vary an assumption to test the output's robustness.

stem: In a financial model, a department's total electricity bill must be divided between the three teams that share the building, in proportion to floor space. This step is:
options: marginal costing of the next unit of work that each team carries out
estimating the variable cost attributable to each of the three teams
cost allocation, dividing a shared cost across the services that use it
an activity-shift impact arising as work moves between the three teams
rationale: Splitting a shared bill across teams by a rule is cost allocation. It is not marginal costing, which concerns the next unit, not variable costing of each team, and not an activity-shift impact, which concerns moving activity between settings.

stem: In financial modelling, the practical difference between a fixed and a variable cost is that:
options: neither cost moves with activity, the two differing only in their overall size
a fixed cost tracks activity closely while a variable cost stays flat throughout
a variable cost tracks activity while a fixed cost holds steady over the range
both costs move with activity, but the fixed cost moves the faster of the two
rationale: The distinction is that variable costs track activity and fixed costs hold steady over the relevant range. The reversed version mislabels both, fixed costs do not move with activity at all, and the two are not simply different sizes of an unchanging cost.

stem: A finance team modelling a procedure divides the full annual running cost of the unit by the number of procedures carried out, to get a cost figure to compare against the national tariff. The figure they have produced is:
options: a fixed cost of running the procedure unit
a marginal cost for each procedure carried out
an activity-shift impact across the settings
a unit cost, the average cost per procedure
rationale: Annual running cost divided by procedures gives a unit cost, the average per procedure. It is not the marginal cost, which is the cost of one more, not the fixed cost, which is only part of the total used here, and not an activity-shift impact.

stem: Validating a model means checking, broadly, whether:
options: its outputs hold up when tested where the right answer is already known
its output shifts noticeably when one input assumption is varied by hand
its predictions exactly match the data the model was originally fitted on
the probabilities it reports mean what they say right across their range
rationale: Validation broadly checks whether the model holds up where the answer can be checked. Matching the fitting data exactly is a sign of overfitting rather than good validation, probabilities meaning what they say is calibration, and seeing how output moves with an assumption is sensitivity analysis.

stem: Calibration of a model concerns whether:
options: the model ranks cases in the correct order, from most to least likely first
the predicted figures, such as a stated probability, mean what they claim
the model continues to hold up on a genuinely different population elsewhere
the output stays robust when one of the input assumptions is changed by hand
rationale: Calibration is whether the reported figures mean what they say, so a stated 30 percent really happens about 30 percent of the time. Ranking cases correctly is discrimination, holding on a different population is external validation, and robustness to a changed assumption is sensitivity analysis.

stem: A sensitivity analysis asks:
options: how much the model's output shifts when an input or assumption is varied
how a set of shared overhead costs ought to be split between several services
whether the model holds up on data that it was not originally fitted against
whether the probabilities it reports match the frequencies actually observed
rationale: A sensitivity analysis varies an input or assumption and watches how the output responds. Probabilities matching observed frequencies is calibration, holding on unseen data is validation, and splitting overheads is cost allocation.

stem: A model can discriminate well yet still be poorly calibrated, meaning that:
options: it ranks cases in the right order, but its reported numbers miss the observed rates
it carries too few predictors to capture the real pattern present in the underlying data
it performs poorly on its own training data, but holds up well on genuinely new data
it reports accurate probabilities, yet ranks the cases in entirely the wrong order
rationale: Discrimination and calibration are separable: a model can order cases correctly while its reported numbers are off. The reverse, accurate numbers with wrong ordering, is not what poor calibration means, failing on training data is a different problem, and too few predictors describes underfitting.

stem: Why is a model never judged on the data it was fitted to?
options: it has already seen that data, so a strong score there may just be memorised noise
the data a model is fitted on contains no errors, which renders the whole test pointless
performance on the data a model was fitted on simply cannot be measured in practice
the fitting data is reliably smaller than the test data, making the result unstable
