When both variables are continuous, roughly normal and linear, Pearson's correlation is the natural choice instead. Measuring association between two categorical variables is a job for a chi-squared test, not a rank correlation. Predicting one variable's value from another goes beyond summarising association and is the work of regression.

stem: The proportional hazards assumption holds the ratio between two groups constant over follow-up. The quantity it keeps in constant ratio is:
options: the probability of having experienced the event by each moment of follow-up
the rate at which the event strikes those who are still at risk, at each moment of follow-up
the overall event rate across the whole follow-up period, taken as a single figure
the proportion of the original group who remain event-free at each moment of follow-up
rationale: A hazard is the instantaneous rate at which the event strikes those who remain at risk, moment by moment, and it is that rate whose ratio proportional hazards holds constant between the groups. The probability of having had the event by a given point is the cumulative risk; keeping its ratio constant would be a proportional-risk condition, a different and generally incompatible assumption. The proportion still event-free is the survival curve, the complement of cumulative risk rather than a rate. A single overall rate for the whole period throws away the moment-by-moment timing that a hazard is defined on.

stem: A group of people is followed over several years, entering and leaving observation at different times. The analyst wants to compare how quickly the event arises between the exposed and unexposed while accounting for each person's differing time at risk. The most appropriate measure is:
options: an odds ratio calculated from the counts of events in each group
a point prevalence measured separately in each group
a risk ratio based on the number of people, setting aside their differing follow-up
a hazard ratio, comparing the groups' event rates across the moments of follow-up
rationale: With people observed for differing lengths of time and the interest in how quickly the event arises, a hazard ratio compares the groups' event rates across follow-up while handling the varying time at risk. An odds ratio compares odds and is not built for uneven follow-up. A point prevalence captures existing cases at a moment and says nothing about how fast events arise. A risk ratio based on the count of people ignores that some were followed far longer than others, which distorts the comparison when follow-up varies.

stem: A t-test is used to assess whether:
options: two categorical variables are associated with one another
the mean of a continuous outcome differs between two groups
the median of a continuous outcome differs between two groups
two continuous variables follow a straight-line relationship
rationale: A t-test compares the mean of a continuous outcome between two groups and asks whether the difference exceeds what sampling variation would explain. Testing whether the median differs instead points to a rank-based test, which does not assume the mean is the right summary. Testing whether two categorical variables are associated is a chi-squared test. Assessing whether two continuous variables move together in a straight line is correlation, which measures association rather than a difference.

stem: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used to test whether:
options: the spread of values within each group is equal across the groups
the means of a continuous outcome differ across three or more groups
the mean outcome follows a consistent upward or downward trend across an ordered sequence of groups
two categorical variables are associated with one another
rationale: Analysis of variance tests whether the means of a continuous outcome differ across three or more groups, without assuming any ordering among them. Testing whether the mean rises or falls in a consistent trend across ordered groups is a test for trend, which looks for a directional pattern rather than any difference at all. Testing whether two categorical variables are associated is a chi-squared test. Testing whether the spread within each group is equal is a check of variance homogeneity, one of ANOVA's assumptions rather than its purpose.

stem: A chi-squared test of independence assesses whether:
options: two categorical variables are associated rather than independent of each other
the mean of a continuous outcome differs between two or more separate groups
two continuous variables follow a straight-line relationship
a single sample's mean differs from a known reference value
rationale: A chi-squared test of independence compares the counts seen in each cross-category with the counts expected if the two categorical variables were unrelated, and a large gap signals association. Comparing the average of a continuous outcome between groups is done with a t-test or analysis of variance. Assessing a straight-line relationship between two continuous variables is correlation. Comparing one sample's mean against a fixed value is a one-sample t-test, again a test about means rather than categorical counts.

stem: Linear (least squares) regression is used to model:
options: a continuous outcome as a straight-line function of one or more predictors
a binary outcome, giving the odds of the outcome for each level of a predictor
a count of events per unit of time, treated as a rate rather than a continuous quantity
the strength of association between two variables without fitting a predictive equation
rationale: Linear regression models a continuous outcome as a straight-line combination of predictors, estimating how the outcome shifts as each predictor changes. Modelling a binary outcome and returning odds is logistic regression, which uses a different link because the outcome is not continuous. Summarising how strongly two variables move together, without fitting an equation to predict one from the other, is correlation. A count of events treated as a rate needs a model built for counts, since ordinary least squares assumes a continuous outcome with roughly constant spread.

stem: Logistic regression is the appropriate model when the outcome is:
options: already summarised as a single proportion, with no predictors involved
a time-to-event outcome, where the timing of events is what matters
continuous, so a straight-line model of its average is wanted
binary, and the analyst wants to relate it to predictors on the odds scale
rationale: Logistic regression suits a binary outcome and expresses how predictors shift the odds of it, yielding odds ratios. A continuous outcome modelled as a straight-line function of predictors calls for linear regression instead. An outcome defined by the time until an event, where timing matters, is handled by survival methods working with hazards. A single proportion with no predictors is a descriptive summary, not something a regression model is needed for.

stem: A team wants to know whether the average waiting time, measured in minutes, differs between three hospital sites. The most appropriate method is:
options: a chi-squared test comparing the sites across waiting-time categories
analysis of variance, comparing mean waiting time across the three sites
a single t-test comparing all three sites at once
a correlation between site and waiting time
rationale: Waiting time is continuous and there are three groups, so analysis of variance, which compares means across three or more groups, is the fit. A chi-squared test would mean cutting the continuous times into categories and testing counts rather than comparing means. A single t-test compares two groups and cannot take three at once. A correlation needs two continuous variables, but site is a set of categories, so it does not apply.

stem: In a time series, the seasonal component refers to:
options: the irregular variation left over once systematic patterns are removed
a sustained one-directional drift upward or downward across the whole series
a pattern that repeats over a fixed, known period, such as the same months each year
the correlation between an observation and the ones immediately before it
rationale: Seasonality is a pattern that recurs over a fixed, known period, such as a winter peak every year, so it is tied to the calendar and repeats. A sustained one-directional drift across the whole series is the trend, which does not repeat. The correlation between an observation and its immediate predecessors is autocorrelation, a property of the series rather than one of its components. The irregular variation remaining once trend and seasonality are removed is the random or residual component.

stem: An analyst fits a straight line to a monthly time series by ordinary regression and finds a statistically significant upward slope. The main reason to be cautious about that significance is that:
options: the upward slope may be an artefact of seasonal peaks rather than a genuine change in level
successive observations are correlated, which ordinary regression treats as independent
the number of time points is usually too small for a regression to be valid
a significant slope shows that the upward movement will continue into the future
rationale: In a time series, successive observations tend to be correlated, and ordinary regression assumes they are independent; ignoring that autocorrelation makes the standard errors too small, so the significance of a fitted trend is overstated. A slope influenced by seasonal peaks is a real concern about the estimate itself, but it is separate from whether the significance can be trusted. The number of time points is not automatically too small, and sample size is not the specific problem here. A significant slope describes the movement seen so far and does not establish that it will continue, which is extrapolation rather than a property of the test.

stem: A process shows small, irregular fluctuations around a steady average, with no single point standing out and no identifiable reason behind the wobble. In statistical process control this is an example of:
options: common-cause variation, the inherent noise of a stable process
measurement error in data collection rather than real process variation
special-cause variation, produced by a specific, identifiable disturbance
a process that is out of control and needs intervention
rationale: Small, irregular fluctuations around a steady average with no assignable reason are the inherent noise of a stable process, which SPC calls common-cause variation. Variation from a specific, identifiable disturbance is special-cause variation, which is not what a steady wobble describes. A process fluctuating within its usual range is in control, so no intervention is warranted. Measurement error is a fault in data collection rather than the genuine process variation being described.

stem: On a control chart, a single point falling outside the control limits is taken to signal:
options: that the process average has been set to the wrong target
ordinary common-cause variation that calls for no action
a likely special cause, worth investigating for what changed
that the sample taken at that point was too small
rationale: A point beyond the control limits is improbable under the process's usual variation alone, so it flags a likely special cause worth investigating. Reading it as ordinary common-cause variation misses that the limits are placed precisely to make such a point unlikely by chance. Treating it as a mis-set target confuses a one-off out-of-limit point with the process being centred in the wrong place. Attributing it to a small sample invents a cause the chart does not point to.

stem: In a fitted linear regression, a slope coefficient of 3 for a predictor means that:
options: the predictor accounts for 3 per cent of the variation in the outcome
the outcome rises by 3 units for each one-unit rise in that predictor, others held fixed
the outcome is expected to be 3 times as large when the predictor is present as when it is absent
for every 3-unit increase in that predictor, the outcome is expected to rise by one unit
rationale: A slope coefficient gives the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit change in that predictor, with the other predictors held constant, so 3 means a rise of three outcome units per unit of predictor. Reading it as the outcome being three times as large treats an additive slope as a multiplier, which would suit a ratio measure rather than a linear coefficient. Reading it as 3 per cent of variation confuses the slope with a measure of fit such as the coefficient of determination. Reading it as a one-unit rise per three-unit increase inverts the coefficient, swapping which variable the change is measured against.

stem: A one-way ANOVA across four groups returns a statistically significant result. This tells you that:
options: the two groups with the highest and lowest means are the ones that differ
at least one group mean differs from the others, but not which ones
every group mean differs from every other group mean
the groups differ in the spread of their values rather than in their means
rationale: A significant ANOVA says the group means are not all equal, so at least one differs, but it does not identify which pairs differ; that needs a follow-up comparison. Concluding that every mean differs from every other over-reads a single overall test. Singling out the highest and lowest as the differing pair assumes a specific contrast the overall test does not license. Reading the result as a difference in spread mistakes what ANOVA compares, which is means, not variability.

stem: A variable acts as a confounder in the relationship between an exposure and an outcome when it:
options: changes the strength or direction of the exposure's effect on the outcome across its own levels
is affected by the exposure and in turn affects the outcome, lying on the causal path between them
is a common consequence of both the exposure and the outcome
is associated with the exposure and independently affects the outcome, off the causal path between them
rationale: A confounder is linked to the exposure and independently affects the outcome while sitting off the causal path from exposure to outcome, so it distorts the crude association and is something to adjust for. A variable on the path, affected by the exposure and then affecting the outcome, is a mediator; adjusting for it would remove part of the very effect being studied. A variable that both the exposure and the outcome influence is a collider; adjusting for it can introduce bias rather than remove it. A variable that alters the size or direction of the effect across its own levels is an effect modifier, which describes how the effect varies rather than distorting it.

stem: Systematic error (bias) differs from random error in that it:
options: reflects the sample being too small to represent the population
varies unpredictably from one sample to the next and averages out as the sample grows
pushes estimates consistently in one direction, so collecting more data does not remove it
shows up as a wider spread of values within the data
rationale: Systematic error moves estimates in a consistent direction, toward or away from the truth, and because it is not a matter of chance, gathering more data does not average it out. Random error, by contrast, varies unpredictably between samples and does shrink as the sample grows. A sample too small to represent the population is a separate issue and does not define bias. Bias does not reveal itself as a wider spread, since a tightly clustered set of values can still be systematically off-target.

stem: In a service evaluation, patients who received a new rehabilitation programme recovered faster than those who did not. Clinicians had tended to offer the programme to younger, fitter patients, who recover faster in any case. The faster recovery in the programme group is most likely explained by:
options: effect modification, since the programme works differently in fitter patients
confounding, since baseline fitness is linked both to being offered the programme and to faster recovery
reverse causation, since faster recovery may have led clinicians to offer the programme
selection bias, since the faster-recovering patients were more likely to remain in the evaluation
rationale: Baseline fitness is associated both with being offered the programme and with faster recovery, and it is not a consequence of the programme, so it confounds the comparison, a confounding-by-indication pattern. Selection bias would arise if faster-recovering patients were differentially retained in or dropped from the evaluation, but the issue here is who was offered the programme, not who stayed in. Reverse causation would require the recovery to have come first and prompted the offer, which the order of events does not support. Effect modification would mean the programme's true effect genuinely differs by fitness, whereas here fitness creates a spurious difference rather than modifying a real one.

stem: In a year-long study, participants who felt worse were more likely to drop out before the final assessment. At the end, those who remained looked healthier on average than the group that started, and the team concluded the intervention had improved health. The main problem is:
options: confounding, since some third factor is distorting the link between the intervention and health
regression to the mean, since extreme early values tend to move toward the average
selection bias, since those who remained are a healthier subset than the group that began
a genuine intervention effect, correctly detected by comparing the start and the end
rationale: Because those who felt worse left before the final assessment, the participants who remained are a healthier subset than the original group, so the end-of-study picture is biased by who stayed, a selection effect from differential drop-out. Confounding would involve a third factor distorting a relationship, but the issue here is the changing make-up of the sample, not a distorted association. Regression to the mean concerns extreme initial measurements drifting toward the average on repeat, which is not what differential drop-out describes. Treating the improvement as a real effect ignores that the comparison is between two differently composed groups.

stem: In causal-diagram (DAG) reasoning, deciding whether to adjust for a particular variable depends on:
options: whether it becomes statistically significant when added to the model
the role it plays in the assumed causal structure of the analysis
whether including it raises the model's overall explained variance
how strongly it is correlated with the outcome in the observed data
rationale: In causal-diagram reasoning, whether to adjust for a variable turns on its role in the assumed causal structure: a confounder should be adjusted for, while a mediator or a collider should be left alone, since adjusting for those introduces bias. Choosing adjustment variables by their correlation with the outcome ignores causal role and can pull in mediators or colliders. Selecting them to raise explained variance optimises fit rather than causal validity. Adding variables just because they reach significance is data-driven selection that disregards the causal structure the diagram exists to make explicit.

stem: A measurement process gives very consistent readings that cluster tightly together, but they all sit some way from the true value. This is best described as:
options: both high precision and high accuracy, since consistent readings must be close to correct
high precision but low accuracy, since the readings agree with each other yet miss the target
low precision but high accuracy, since the readings scatter widely around the true value
random error, which would make the readings vary unpredictably rather than cluster
rationale: Readings that cluster tightly are precise, but if they sit away from the true value they are inaccurate, so the process is precise yet biased; consistency and correctness are separate properties. The inverse description, widely scattered readings centred on the truth, would be accurate but imprecise, the opposite situation. Treating consistent readings as necessarily close to correct is the very error the example exposes, since a systematic shift can be perfectly consistent. Random error would show as unpredictable scatter, not a tight cluster offset from the target, so it does not describe this pattern.

stem: Across primary-school children, those with larger shoe sizes tend to have higher reading scores. The most likely reason this is not a causal relationship is that:
options: a common cause, the child's age, raises both shoe size and reading ability
larger shoe size directly improves reading ability through some unmeasured mechanism
the pattern is a chance finding that a larger sample would remove
shoe size or reading was recorded inaccurately, creating a false link
rationale: Older children tend to have both larger feet and better reading, so age is a common cause producing an association between shoe size and reading without either affecting the other, a spurious correlation from a shared cause. Claiming shoe size directly improves reading reads a shared-cause pattern as a direct effect. Calling it a chance finding ignores that the association is real and would persist, being driven by age. Inaccurate recording would distort the figures, but the association here is genuine and explained by age, not by mis-measurement.

stem: In the context of causal reasoning, covariation between two variables means that they:
options: appear to move together only as an artefact of how they were measured
are statistically associated, so changes in one accompany changes in the other
move independently, with no association between them
change together, but only because one of them directly causes the other
rationale: Covariation means the two variables are statistically associated, so that they tend to change together; it is the observed co-movement itself, which may or may not be causal. Saying they change together only when one causes the other collapses covariation into causation, when an association can also arise from a common cause or from chance. Variables that move independently show no covariation at all, the opposite of the concept. An apparent link created by measurement error is an artefact rather than genuine covariation.

stem: The recorded number of cases of a condition jumps sharply in the same month a new coding system is introduced. This is most likely:
options: a data-quality artefact, as the coding change altered how cases were recorded
a genuine rise in the true incidence of the condition
confounding by a third factor linked to both the condition and the coding change
selection bias in how cases entered the dataset
rationale: A jump that coincides with a new coding system points to a data-quality artefact: the recording of cases changed, not their true frequency. Reading it as a genuine rise in incidence takes the artefact at face value. Confounding concerns a third factor distorting an exposure-outcome association, not a coding-driven jump. Selection bias concerns how cases enter a sample, whereas here the issue is how existing cases were coded.

stem: An audit of a clinic's records finds that outcome data are missing far more often for patients who did badly than for those who did well. An analysis using only the complete records is most likely to:
options: understate how good the outcomes are, because complete records favour worse cases
be biased only if the total amount of missing data is large
overstate how good the outcomes are, as poor outcomes are disproportionately missing
be unaffected, since missing data reduce precision but not the estimate
rationale: When poor outcomes are missing more often, the complete records over-represent good outcomes, so an analysis restricted to them overstates how well patients did; this is a data-quality artefact from data missing in a way related to the outcome. The inverse claim, that complete records favour worse cases, reverses the direction of the missingness. Treating the analysis as unaffected assumes missingness only costs precision, but missingness tied to the outcome shifts the estimate. And it is the pattern of missingness, not merely its volume, that creates the bias, so a small amount missing systematically can still distort the result.

stem: The standard deviation of a set of measurements describes:
options: the proportion of values that fall above the mean
how much individual values typically spread around their mean
how precisely the mean itself has been estimated
the gap between the smallest and the largest value in the set
rationale: The standard deviation summarises how far individual values typically lie from their mean, capturing the spread of the data. How precisely the mean has been estimated is the standard error, which shrinks with sample size while the standard deviation does not. The gap between the smallest and largest values is the range, a cruder measure sensitive to extremes. The proportion of values above the mean is a feature of the distribution's shape, not a measure of spread.

stem: The standard error of a mean describes:
options: how much the sample mean itself would vary from one sample to the next
the largest error any single measurement could plausibly contain
the exact difference between the sample mean and the true population mean
how much individual values spread around the mean within one sample
rationale: The standard error captures how much the sample mean would vary if sampling were repeated, so it measures the precision of the estimate and shrinks as the sample grows. The spread of individual values within one sample is the standard deviation, which describes the data rather than the estimate. The largest error a single measurement could hold is not what the standard error means; it concerns the mean, not one reading. The actual gap between the sample mean and the true mean is the estimate's error, which is unknown, whereas the standard error quantifies expected variability, not that specific gap.

stem: The key difference between the standard deviation and the standard error is that:
options: the standard deviation applies to proportions and the standard error to means
they measure the same thing, but the standard error is the version used for larger samples
the standard deviation falls as the sample grows, while the standard error stays fixed
the standard deviation measures the spread, the standard error the precision of an estimate
rationale: The standard deviation describes how spread out the data are and does not systematically shrink with more data, whereas the standard error describes how precisely a statistic such as the mean is estimated and does shrink as the sample grows. Treating them as the same measure differing only by sample size misses that they describe different things, data spread versus estimate precision. Saying the standard deviation falls with sample size while the standard error stays fixed reverses their behaviour. Restricting the standard deviation to proportions and the standard error to means invents a distinction that does not exist, since both apply across measures.

stem: A 95% confidence interval for a mean is best understood as:
options: a range that has a 95% probability of containing the true mean, for this particular interval
a range within which 95% of the individual data values fall
a plausible range for the true mean, from a method that captures it in 95% of repeated samples
the range within which the sample mean itself is known to lie
rationale: A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that, over many repeated samples, captures the true mean 95% of the time, so it gives a range of plausible values for that mean. Saying this particular interval has a 95% probability of holding the true mean is the common misreading; in the standard framework the true mean is fixed and the interval either contains it or not, and the 95% refers to the procedure. A range holding 95% of individual values describes the spread of the data, not the precision of the mean. The sample mean is simply the centre of the interval and is already known, so an interval is not needed to locate it.

stem: Sampling variability refers to:
options: the spread of individual values within a single sample
the way the true population value itself changes over time
the way an estimate such as a mean varies from sample to sample
a systematic error introduced by how the sample was selected
rationale: Sampling variability is the sample-to-sample variation in an estimate that arises because each random sample includes different individuals, and it is what the standard error quantifies. It is not the population value changing over time; the true value is treated as fixed while the estimate varies. A systematic error from how the sample was chosen is selection bias, a directional problem rather than chance variation. The spread of individual values within one sample is the standard deviation, a property of the data rather than of the estimate across samples.

stem: A small study reports a treatment effect with a very wide 95% confidence interval running from a large benefit to a slight harm. The most reasonable interpretation is that:
options: the treatment definitely works, because the interval includes a large benefit
the treatment has no effect, because the interval is wide
the result is invalid and should be discarded
the study is too imprecise to judge the effect, as the range spans benefit to harm
rationale: A wide interval spanning benefit to harm means the data are consistent with a broad range of possibilities, so the study is too imprecise to pin the effect down rather than showing anything definite. Reading the width as evidence of no effect confuses imprecision with a null result; the interval does not centre on no effect. Taking the benefit end as proof the treatment works cherry-picks one edge of a range that also includes harm. Discarding the result as invalid overreacts, since a wide interval reflects low precision, often from a small sample, not invalidity.

stem: An estimate is found to be both imprecise and biased. Which pairing of problem and remedy is correct?
options: a larger sample reduces the imprecision, but the bias must be tackled at its source
the bias can be reduced by widening the confidence interval to reflect the uncertainty
both the imprecision and the bias can be reduced by collecting a larger sample
both problems can be reduced by repeating the measurement and averaging the results
rationale: Imprecision comes from sampling variability and falls as the sample grows, so more data reduces it; bias is a systematic error that a larger sample does not remove, so it must be addressed at its source, such as a fault in measurement or design. Expecting more data to reduce the bias too is the common mistake, since averaging more observations narrows the spread but leaves a systematic shift in place. Repeating and averaging likewise improves only the precision. Widening the confidence interval reports more uncertainty but does nothing to remove a systematic error.

stem: A defining property of the normal distribution is that:
options: it is symmetric about its mean, though its mean typically falls a little above its median
it is symmetric about its mean, so that its mean, median and mode all coincide
it is bell-shaped, with roughly equal numbers of values in every equal-width interval across its range
it is bell-shaped, with almost all of its values lying within one standard deviation of the mean
rationale: The normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, and because of that symmetry its mean, median and mode fall at the same point. Saying the mean falls a little above the median contradicts symmetry, since that upward pull is a feature of a right-skewed distribution. Saying every equal-width interval holds roughly equal numbers of values describes a flat, uniform distribution, whereas the normal is densest near the centre and thins toward the tails. And only about two-thirds of its values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, with almost all within three, so "almost all within one" understates the spread.

stem: The Poisson distribution is typically used to model:
options: the count of rare independent events in a fixed interval of time or space
a continuous outcome with a long tail toward high values
the number of successes in a fixed number of separate yes/no trials
the spread of a continuous measurement that is symmetric about its mean
rationale: The Poisson distribution models counts of independent events in a fixed interval of time or space, suited to relatively rare events such as new cases arising in a population. A symmetric continuous measurement is described by the normal distribution. The number of successes across a fixed number of yes/no trials follows the binomial distribution. A continuous outcome with a long upper tail is a skewed distribution, not a count model.

stem: In a strongly right-skewed distribution, such as household income:
options: the mean is pulled above the median by the long tail, so the median is more typical
the distribution is symmetric, since skewness does not affect the central values
the median is pulled above the mean by the long upper tail
the mean and the median are equal, as they are in any distribution
rationale: A long upper tail drags the mean upward more than the median, so in a right-skewed distribution the mean sits above the median and the median often gives a better sense of a typical value. The mean and median coincide only in a symmetric distribution, not a skewed one. Saying the median exceeds the mean reverses the direction of the pull in right skew. Describing the distribution as symmetric contradicts its being skewed.

stem: The sensitivity of a diagnostic test is:
options: the proportion of people who truly have the condition that the test correctly identifies as positive
the proportion of people testing positive who truly have the condition
the proportion of people testing negative who truly do not have the condition
the proportion of people who truly do not have the condition that the test correctly identifies as negative
rationale: Sensitivity is the share of those who genuinely have the condition whom the test correctly flags as positive, so it measures detection among true cases. The share of those without the condition correctly called negative is specificity. The share of positive testers who truly have the condition is the positive predictive value. The share of negative testers who truly lack it is the negative predictive value.

stem: The specificity of a diagnostic test is:
options: the proportion of people testing positive who truly have the condition
the proportion of people who truly have the condition that the test correctly identifies as positive
the proportion of people testing negative who truly do not have the condition
the proportion of people who truly do not have the condition that the test correctly identifies as negative
rationale: Specificity is the share of those who genuinely do not have the condition whom the test correctly clears as negative, so it measures correct exclusion among true non-cases. The share of those with the condition correctly called positive is sensitivity. The share of negative testers who truly lack the condition is the negative predictive value. The share of positive testers who truly have it is the positive predictive value.

stem: The probability that someone who tests positive genuinely has the condition is captured by a test's:
options: specificity
sensitivity
negative predictive value
positive predictive value
rationale: The probability that a positive result is a true case is the positive predictive value, which reads from the test result back to disease status. Sensitivity runs the other way, from those who truly have the condition to a positive result. Specificity concerns true non-cases and negative results. The negative predictive value concerns those who test negative, not positive.

stem: A false positive and a false negative differ in that:
options: both are correct results, one identifying a case and the other a non-case
a false negative is what lowers a test's specificity, while a false positive is what lowers its sensitivity
a false positive is a positive test in someone without the condition, while a false negative is a negative test in someone who has it
a false positive is a negative test in someone with the condition, while a false negative is a positive test in someone without it
rationale: A false positive is a positive test in a person who does not have the condition, and a false negative is a negative test in a person who does; these are the test's two kinds of error. Defining a false positive as a negative test in someone who has the condition, and a false negative as a positive test in someone without it, reverses the two. Calling both correct results misreads the word "false," which marks an error in each. And the links to the metrics run the other way: a false negative, a missed case, is what lowers sensitivity, while a false positive, a false alarm, is what lowers specificity.

stem: When the same test is used in a population where the condition is rarer, which of its measures changes?
options: the predictive values change, while sensitivity and specificity do not
none of the measures change, since they are fixed properties of the test
all four measures change in proportion to the prevalence
sensitivity and specificity change, while the predictive values stay the same
rationale: Predictive values depend on how common the condition is, so moving the test to a lower-prevalence population lowers the positive predictive value and raises the negative predictive value, while sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test itself and stay the same. Saying sensitivity and specificity change while predictive values hold reverses which measures are prevalence-dependent. Saying all four change treats sensitivity and specificity as prevalence-dependent, which they are not. Saying none change ignores that predictive values shift with prevalence.

stem: A clinician needs a first-line test for a serious condition where missing a true case would be dangerous, so no case should be overlooked. The most important property for this test is:
options: high positive predictive value
high negative predictive value
high sensitivity
high specificity
rationale: When missing a case is the danger, the test must catch nearly all true cases, so high sensitivity matters most, and a negative result from a sensitive test reliably rules the condition out. High specificity minimises false alarms, which suits ruling a condition in rather than ensuring none is missed. A high positive predictive value and a high negative predictive value are both desirable, but they depend on how common the condition is as well as on the test, so they are not properties the test can be built for directly, whereas sensitivity is intrinsic to the test.

stem: A screening programme is concerned that too many healthy people are being sent for invasive and costly follow-up after a positive screen. To reduce this, it should prioritise a test with:
options: high sensitivity, so that few people with the condition screen negative
a high negative predictive value, so that a negative screen is usually correct
high specificity, so that few people without the condition screen positive
a high false-positive rate, so that borderline cases are flagged for review
rationale: To cut the number of healthy people wrongly sent for follow-up, the programme needs few false positives, so it should prioritise high specificity, which correctly clears true non-cases. High sensitivity reduces missed cases but does nothing to limit false alarms among the healthy. A high negative predictive value concerns how far a negative screen can be trusted, not how many healthy people screen positive. A high false-positive rate would worsen the problem by flagging more healthy people, so seeking it is the opposite of what is needed.

stem: Raising the positivity threshold of a test, so that a stronger result is needed to call someone positive, will typically:
options: leave both sensitivity and specificity unchanged
increase both sensitivity and specificity
reduce specificity but increase sensitivity
increase specificity but reduce sensitivity
rationale: A higher threshold means fewer people are called positive, so more true non-cases are correctly cleared, raising specificity, but more true cases are missed, lowering sensitivity; the two move in opposite directions. Raising both at once cannot be done by moving the threshold, since it trades one for the other. Saying specificity falls while sensitivity rises reverses the effect of a stricter cut-off. And the threshold does affect both, so saying they are unchanged is wrong.

stem: In a screening programme, "uptake" refers to:
options: the proportion of the eligible population who actually take part in the screening
the proportion of those screened who are found to have the condition
the proportion of positive screens that are later confirmed as true cases
the proportion of those screened who go on to receive treatment
rationale: Uptake is the share of the eligible population who come forward and take part, so it measures participation and matters because low uptake limits a programme's reach and can skew who is covered. The share of those screened found to have the condition is the detection rate, or yield, a different measure. The share of positive screens later confirmed is the positive predictive value. The share going on to receive treatment is a downstream measure of the care pathway, not participation in screening.

stem: An age-standardised rate for a population represents:
options: the population's crude rate after its oldest and youngest age groups are set aside
the rate the population would have if its age structure matched a chosen standard
the average of the population's age-specific rates, giving each age group equal weight
the rate observed in the age group that contributes the most cases
rationale: A standardised rate is a hypothetical figure: it is the rate a population would show if its age structure matched an agreed standard, which is what lets different populations be compared fairly. It is not the crude rate with certain age groups set aside, since standardisation reweights every age group rather than dropping any. It is not an equal-weighted average of the age-specific rates, because the standard structure gives each age group its own weight. And it is not the rate in whichever age group contributes the most cases, since all age groups feed in, weighted by the standard.

stem: A crude rate for a whole population can mislead when two populations are compared because it:
options: counts only formally diagnosed cases, so milder cases are missed
is expressed per head of population, so a larger population will show a lower rate
reflects the population's age or other structure rather than the underlying risk
removes the effect of age, making the two populations look artificially similar
rationale: A crude rate lumps the whole population together, so it is shaped by the age or other structure of that population, and two populations with different structures can differ on the crude rate even at the same underlying risk. Being expressed per head does not mean a larger population shows a lower rate; a rate is a ratio and does not fall simply because the population is bigger. Missing milder, undiagnosed cases is an ascertainment problem that affects any rate, crude or standardised, so it is not what makes the crude rate specifically misleading across populations. And a crude rate does not remove the effect of age, which is precisely what standardisation, not the crude rate, does.

stem: After standardising the rates of two areas to the same population structure, a difference that remains between them is best interpreted as:
options: a difference in underlying risk, now that structure has been accounted for
an artefact of standardisation that should be disregarded
proof that conditions in the higher area are causing the difference
a difference still driven by the two areas' differing age structures
rationale: Standardisation removes the effect of differing population structures, so a difference that remains reflects a difference in underlying risk rather than composition. It does not by itself prove that conditions in the higher area cause the difference, since standardisation adjusts for structure, not for every other factor that might differ between the areas. It is not an artefact to disregard; the remaining difference is the meaningful signal standardisation exists to expose. And it is not still driven by differing age structures, since standardising to a common structure is exactly what removes that effect.

stem: An age-standardised rate adjusts for:
options: differences in the underlying risk of the condition between populations
differences in the total size of the populations being compared
differences in the accuracy of case recording between populations
differences in the age structure of the populations being compared
rationale: Age-standardisation removes the effect of differing age structures, so two populations can be compared without age composition driving the difference. It does not adjust for the total size of the populations, since rates already account for size through their denominators. It does not correct differences in how accurately cases are recorded, which is a data-quality matter. And it does not remove differences in underlying risk; those are exactly what a fair comparison is meant to reveal once age is accounted for.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes direct from indirect standardisation?
options: both apply the same standard rates to the same standard structure, and differ only in how the result is presented
direct applies standard rates to each population's own structure, while indirect applies each population's own age-specific rates to a standard structure
direct standardisation adjusts for differences in age, while indirect standardisation adjusts for differences in population size
direct applies each population's own age-specific rates to a standard structure, while indirect applies standard rates to each population's own structure
rationale: In direct standardisation each population's own age-specific rates are applied to one standard age structure, so the resulting rates differ only because of the rates; in indirect standardisation a standard set of rates is applied to each population's own structure, producing a ratio of observed to expected cases. The option that applies standard rates to each population's own structure while calling that the direct method swaps the two. Saying both apply the same rates to the same structure is wrong, since that would make them identical, which they are not. And indirect standardisation does not adjust for population size: both methods adjust for age structure, differing only in which component, the rates or the structure, is taken as the standard.

stem: Two regions have the same age-specific death rates, but region A has a much older population than region B. Comparing the two, you would expect that:
options: region B has the higher crude rate, because it has more younger people
the crude and age-standardised rates are equal in both regions
region A has the higher crude rate and also the higher age-standardised rate
region A has the higher crude rate, while their standardised rates are about equal
rationale: With identical age-specific rates, the two regions differ only in age structure, so region A's older population gives it more deaths per head overall and a higher crude rate, while standardising to a common structure makes their rates about equal, revealing the same underlying risk. Saying region A also has the higher standardised rate misses that the age-specific rates are identical, so standardisation equalises them. Saying region B has the higher crude rate reverses the effect of its younger population. Saying crude and standardised rates are equal in both ignores that age structure lifts region A's crude rate above its standardised one.

stem: Two areas' age-standardised rates can be compared directly only when:
options: the two areas had the same age structure to begin with
each has been standardised to its own most recent population
both have been standardised to the same standard population
the two areas have the same total population size
rationale: A directly standardised rate depends on the standard structure it was calculated against, so two such rates can be compared only if both used the same standard; otherwise a difference could come from the choice of standard rather than from the areas. Standardising each area to its own population reintroduces exactly the structural differences standardisation is meant to remove. Equal total population size is beside the point, since rates already account for size. And if the two areas had shared an age structure to begin with there would be nothing to standardise, so that is not the condition for comparing standardised rates.

stem: Crude and standardised rates suit different jobs. For which of these is a crude rate the more appropriate measure?
options: comparing two districts whose populations differ greatly in age
ranking all the districts in the country from highest to lowest risk
judging whether a single district's rate has truly risen over the past thirty years, as its population has aged
estimating how many cases a single district must resource this year, to plan its local services
rationale: A crude rate gives the actual number of cases relative to the real population, so it is the right basis for resourcing a single district's services here and now. Comparing two districts whose populations differ greatly in age needs a standardised rate, so that the age gap does not drive the comparison. Judging whether one district's rate has truly risen over thirty years also needs standardisation, since the population has aged over that time and a crude rise could reflect ageing rather than a real change in risk. And ranking all the districts by risk is a comparison across places with different age structures, which again calls for standardised rates.
